clues.ahaFactoid: Clemons first met Springsteen on a stormy Asbury Park night in 1971—supposedly blowing the club door right off its hinges when he walked in!

clues.stem: Decades after its 1985 release, Kate Bush’s "Running Up That Hill" rocketed back into the Billboard Top 5 in 2022 after starring in what Netflix sci-fi hit?
clues.ahaFactoid: Played repeatedly to save Max Mayfield from Vecna in Season 4, the track earned Kate Bush three new Guinness World Records 37 years later!

clues.stem: In July 1985, Freddie Mercury hijacked which towering London stadium for 21 unforgettable minutes during Live Aid?
clues.ahaFactoid: Queen’s sound engineer quietly nudged Wembley’s master limiter past the red line during Radio Ga Ga so Mercury’s "Ay-Oh!" echoed around the world!

clues.stem: Before winning four Grammys in 1972 for her landmark solo LP, Carole King co-wrote hits like "Will You Love Me Tomorrow" inside what Manhattan hit factory?
clues.ahaFactoid: Working alongside Gerry Goffin at 1650 Broadway and Aldon Music next door, Carole King cranked out timeless teen standards at age 18!

clues.stem: Deaf by the 1824 Vienna premiere of his Ninth Symphony, Ludwig van Beethoven set the famous choral finale to a poem by which German writer?
clues.ahaFactoid: Friedrich Schiller wrote "An die Freude" (Ode to Joy) in 1785, and Beethoven carried the dream of setting it to symphony for thirty years!

clues.stem: Premiering in Paris in May 1913 with Nijinsky’s stomping choreography, which composer’s "The Rite of Spring" provoked fistfights and shouted jeers in the theater?
clues.ahaFactoid: Its brutal asymmetrical rhythms and screeching opening bassoon practically split the audience in two—yet reshaped 20th-century classical and film music overnight!

clues.stem: Memphis Bulletin, 1955: Inspired by a proud dancer snapping "Don’t step on my shoes!", rockabilly pioneer [ _____ ] recorded "Blue Suede Shoes" at Sun Studio.
clues.ahaFactoid: Perkins’s infectious bounce became Sun Records’ very first million-selling record—soon covered by Elvis Presley across national TV!

clues.stem: Concert Wire, 1965: Performing before 55,600 screaming fans at New York’s [ _____ ], The Beatles launched the modern era of giant stadium rock tours.
clues.ahaFactoid: Amplifiers barely reached 100 watts in 1965, so the Fab Four literally couldn’t hear themselves play over the jet-engine roar of 55,000 teenagers!

clues.stem: Tampa Broadcast, 1991: Backed by the Florida Orchestra in a white tracksuit, [ _____ ] delivered a soaring "Star-Spangled Banner" still hailed as the Super Bowl’s finest.
clues.ahaFactoid: Houston’s 4/4 arrangement actually re-entered the Billboard Hot 100 twice—climbing to #20 in 1991 and #6 in 2001!

clues.stem: New York Wire, 2024: Wrapping up an unmatched monthly streak across a full decade, Piano Man [ _____ ] closed his 150th career concert at Madison Square Garden.
clues.ahaFactoid: Since debuting at the Garden in 1978, Billy Joel sold out more than two million tickets at Manhattan’s most famous arena!

clues.stem: London Dispatch, 1973: Stunning weeping fans at Hammersmith Odeon, [ _____ ] announced onstage that "it’s the last show we’ll ever do," retiring alter ego Ziggy Stardust.
clues.ahaFactoid: Even Bowie’s own Spiders from Mars backing band had no warning until he grabbed the mic before closing with "Rock ’n’ Roll Suicide"!

clues.stem: Tech Music Wire, 2000: Discovering an unfinished demo circulating online for free, heavy metal giant [ _____ ] famously sued file-sharing pioneer Napster.
clues.ahaFactoid: Lars Ulrich delivered boxes containing over 300,000 usernames straight to Napster’s San Mateo office—forever changing how the record industry fought digital piracy!

clues.stem: Country Dispatch, 1958: Watching a prison concert from the inmates’ front row in San Quentin inspired future country giant [ _____ ] to turn his life toward songwriting.
clues.ahaFactoid: Nine years later, Merle Haggard stepped back onto San Quentin’s stage—this time as a chart-topping star invited to play with California’s governor watching!

clues.stem: Grammy Wire, 2004: Powered by "Hey Ya!" and "The Way You Move," Atlanta duo [ _____ ] became the first pure hip-hop act to win Album of the Year.
clues.ahaFactoid: Big Boi and Andre 3000’s sprawling double disc essentially teamed two solo albums under one roof—earning six Grammy nominations and three wins!

clues.stem: Classical Dispatch, 1955: Humming softly over a squeaky folding chair in a 30th Street studio, Canadian pianist [ _____ ] electrified the world with Bach’s Goldberg Variations.
clues.ahaFactoid: Quitting live concerts permanently at age 31, Glenn Gould returned to record the Goldberg Variations a second time in 1981 at a far slower, brooding tempo!

clues.stem: Archivist Memo, 1952: Compiling 84 forgotten 78 rpm blues and Appalachian ballads onto six LPs, eccentric filmmaker [ _____ ] sparked the American folk revival.
clues.ahaFactoid: Released by Moe Asch’s Folkways label, Harry Smith’s Anthology of American Folk Music became the secret bible for Bob Dylan, Joan Baez, and Jerry Garcia!

clues.stem: Shot from behind against bold red-and-white stripes, a blue-jeaned rock star wears a faded white tee with a crimson baseball cap tucked in his back pocket:
clues.ahaFactoid: Photographer Annie Leibovitz snapped that iconic red-cap silhouette for Bruce Springsteen’s 1984 smash—though fans joked he looked like he was facing the flag!

clues.stem: Printed cleanly across a stark white square sleeve by Andy Warhol, a bright yellow tropical fruit invited 1967 buyers to "Peel Slowly and See":
clues.ahaFactoid: Early vinyl pressings of The Velvet Underground & Nico actually featured a peelable yellow sticker revealing a pink fruit underneath!

clues.stem: Black V-striped crimson leather shoulders glowing under amber streetlamps while yellow-eyed zombies burst out of misty graves in synchronized step:
clues.ahaFactoid: Costume designer Deborah Nadoolman gave Jackson’s Thriller jacket broad triangular shoulders to make his slim silhouette look heroic against dark alleys!

clues.stem: Spangled head to toe in a glittering blue-and-white sequined Dodgers baseball uniform and feathered sunglasses behind a grand piano before 55,000 fans:
clues.ahaFactoid: Bob Mackie stitched that dazzling sequined #1 jersey for Elton John’s legendary October 1975 two-night triumph at Los Angeles’s Dodger Stadium!

clues.stem: Tilting his floppy-eared terrier head quizzically in front of a brass phonograph horn, a loyal black-and-white pup listens closely to "His Master’s Voice":
clues.ahaFactoid: Painter Francis Barraud painted his late brother’s terrier Nipper listening intently to an old Edison cylinder phonograph back in 1898!

clues.stem: Gleaming like carved ebony sculpture on a black gloss backdrop, a flat-top diva balances impossibly on one tiptoe holding a microphone—which 1985 sleeve?
clues.ahaFactoid: Photographer Jean-Paul Goude actually cut and spliced multiple Polaroid shots together to create Grace Jones’s anatomically impossible arabesque!

clues.stem: Caught mid-air in grainy black-and-white motion blur, which Clash bassist raises his Fender Precision Bass high to smash it straight into the Palladium stage?
clues.ahaFactoid: Photographer Pennie Smith hated the out-of-focus shot at first, yet Joe Strummer insisted it became the greatest rock sleeve of all time!

clues.stem: Stacked white jagged mountain peaks floating inside a stark matte-black sleeve—actually radio waves pulsing out of the first discovered pulsar star:
clues.ahaFactoid: Designer Peter Saville lifted the 1970 astronomical chart of pulsar CP 1919 straight out of the Cambridge Encyclopedia of Astronomy for Joy Division’s 1979 debut!

clues.stem: Cropped ultra-tight in deep cobalt shadows with bold lowercase Helvetica lettering kissing the edge—which designer defined Blue Note Records’ iconic jazz sleeves?
clues.ahaFactoid: Pairing Francis Wolff’s smoky studio session photos with audacious Swiss typography, Reid Miles designed nearly 500 classic Blue Note covers!

clues.stem: Four string musicians strapped separately inside four hovering helicopters with live rotor microphones beaming quartet chords into a concert hall below:
clues.ahaFactoid: Avant-garde German composer Karlheinz Stockhausen premiered his wild 1995 Helicopter String Quartet in Amsterdam—inspired by a vivid dream!

He sawed legs off his pianos

clues.ahaFactoid: In famous 2012–2017 blind tests in Paris and Indianapolis, world-class soloists frequently preferred brand-new violins over multimillion-dollar Stradivariuses!

clues.stem: Grammy Klaxon! Three of these pop-scandal facts are completely true, while one twist about Milli Vanilli’s 1990 fallout is false. Spot the myth!
choices: A skipped tape exposed them live
They got a Best New Artist nod
Real singers worked in the studio

clues.stem: Baroque Klaxon! Three of these J.S. Bach milestones are historical fact, while one claim about his 1700s fame is upside down. Spot the myth!
choices: Bach was mostly famous as a violinist
His son Carl outsold him in 1760s
clues.ahaFactoid: During his lifetime, Bach was celebrated across Germany primarily as a phenomenal church organist and keyboard improviser—far more than as a composer or violinist!

clues.stem: Songwriter ear test: which classic musical scale quality generally gives melodies a bright, sunny, joyful lift rather than a moody, wistful ache?
clues.ahaFactoid: Lowering the third note by a single half-step transforms a bright Major chord into a soulful Minor chord instantly!

clues.stem: Studio session showdown: which famous 1990s live album series stripped rock stars down to wooden guitars, pianos, and cello without distortion amps?
clues.ahaFactoid: Eric Clapton’s acoustic "Layla" and Nirvana’s haunting 1993 MTV Unplugged in New York proved great songs shine without stadium stacks!

clues.stem: 45 rpm record showdown: when bands flipped a single vinyl record over to hide a quirky experimental track or future smash like "I Will Survive," what was that flip side called?
clues.ahaFactoid: Gloria Gaynor’s "I Will Survive" and Queen’s "We Will Rock You" both grew into world-conquering anthems after starting life on the B-side!

clues.stem: Choir riser showdown: which standard classical singing voice sits at the HIGHEST female pitch range?
clues.ahaFactoid: From the Italian "sopra" ("above"), sopranos soar over the top of choral harmonies—just as tenors crown the high end of male voices!

clues.stem: Antique turntable split: before vinyl LPs standardized around 1948, brittle early 1920s–40s shellac discs spun at what brisk speed?
clues.ahaFactoid: Spinning at 78 revolutions per minute meant a 10-inch shellac disc held barely three minutes of audio per side—explaining why pop songs still hover near three minutes!

clues.stem: Scale showdown: play ONLY the black keys on a piano and you’ll automatically improvise in what ancient five-note scale loved across blues, Motown, and folk?
clues.ahaFactoid: With no harsh half-step clashes anywhere, the five-note pentatonic scale lets almost any note sound soulful over a blues progression!

clues.stem: 1960s studio split: Brian Wilson mixed "Pet Sounds" specifically in which single-speaker format because he was deaf in one ear and loved unified punch?
clues.ahaFactoid: Having lost hearing in his right ear as a child, Brian Wilson insisted mono let every listener hear the exact wall-of-sound blend he heard in the studio!

clues.stem: Vocal booth showdown: which rugged, battery-free microphone type (like the stage classic Shure SM58) handles screaming rock concerts without needing 48V phantom power?
clues.ahaFactoid: Using a sturdy moving coil and magnet rather than fragile charged plates, dynamic mics can survive dropped stages and roaring guitar cabinets!

clues.stem: Harmony showdown: church choirs sing "A-men" at the close of hymns over a IV-to-I chord shift—what classic nickname belongs to that warm cadence?
clues.ahaFactoid: The Plagal ("Amen") cadence also closes pop classics like The Beatles’ "Let It Be" and Otis Redding’s "(Sittin’ On) The Dock of the Bay"!

clues.stem: Tuning showdown: barbershop quartets ring eerie "overtone lock" chords by subtly bending thirds and fifths into pure whole-number ratios—what system is that?
clues.ahaFactoid: Because equal-tempered pianos slightly flatten fifths and sharpen major thirds, vocalists and string quartets naturally gravitate toward pure just intonation!

clues.stem: Peek inside a modern U.S. ATM or bank teller’s drawer: which printed paper banknote carries the HIGHEST face value still printed for everyday circulation?
clues.ahaFactoid: Since 1969, the Federal Reserve stopped issuing $500, $1,000, $5,000, and $10,000 notes—making Benjamin Franklin’s $100 bill the top everyday note!

clues.stem: Open a classic U.S. Monopoly box and pick the SINGLE highest-value paper bill included in the banker’s tray:
clues.ahaFactoid: Classic Monopoly tops out at orange $500 notes—providing $20,580 in total bank money inside every standard set!

clues.stem: Empty a handful of standard U.S. pocket change onto a table: which everyday coin has the WIDEST metal diameter?
clues.ahaFactoid: At 24.26 millimeters across, a Washington quarter easily beats a nickel (21.21 mm), penny (19.05 mm), and tiny dime (17.91 mm)!

clues.stem: After enjoying friendly sit-down restaurant table service in the United States, which gratuity rate represents the HIGHER traditional tip standard vs. bare minimum?
clues.ahaFactoid: While 15% was the longtime post-war norm, 18% to 20% pre-tax became the standard courtesy benchmark for good American sit-down service!

clues.stem: Check the embossed account digits across the front of standard U.S. payment cards: how many digits does an American Express card print (fewer than Visa/Mastercard)?
clues.ahaFactoid: While Visa, Mastercard, and Discover print 16-digit card numbers, American Express uses 15 digits—starting with a 3 instead of 4, 5, or 6!

clues.stem: Applying for a home loan with standard FICO scores ranging from 300 to 850, which score unlocks the LOWER, friendlier interest rate?
clues.ahaFactoid: Lenders reserve their lowest mortgage rates for borrowers above 740–760—saving tens of thousands in interest over a 30-year loan!

clues.stem: Roll up coins at the bank: how many U.S. quarters fill a standard $10 paper coin wrapper?
clues.ahaFactoid: Forty quarters equal $10.00—while a standard dime roll holds 50 coins ($5.00), a nickel roll holds 40 ($2.00), and a penny roll holds 50 ($0.50)!

clues.stem: Because people crease, spend, and stash them in piggy banks rather than wear them out daily, which U.S. banknote stays in circulation LONGER (averaging ~15+ years)?
clues.ahaFactoid: Crisp $1 bills wear out in roughly 6.6 years from constant cash-register friction, whereas $100 bills often sit untouched for over 20 years!

clues.stem: Feel the ridged coin edges in your pocket: which U.S. coin packs MORE tiny vertical grooves ("reeds") around its rim—119 vs. 118?
clues.ahaFactoid: Both dimes and quarters carry reeded edges originally meant to stop coin-clippers shaving silver—and a quarter holds just one extra reed (119 vs. 118)!

clues.stem: Which common household borrowing product typically charges a MUCH HIGHER annual interest rate (APR) if you carry an unpaid balance?
clues.ahaFactoid: Store and retail credit cards routinely charge 25%–30%+ APR—four or five times higher than typical home mortgages!

clues.stem: Compare corporate giants on Wall Street: which famous tech parent company reached a MUCH HIGHER market valuation (over $2 trillion)?
clues.ahaFactoid: Google parent Alphabet joined the $2 trillion Wall Street club—more than twenty times larger than footwear titan Nike or coffee chain Starbucks!

clues.stem: Which major U.S. financial role actually collects a LOWER official government salary (~$203,500) than a top private Wall Street bank CEO?
clues.ahaFactoid: Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell earns a modest public-servant salary around $203,500—while major Wall Street CEOs regularly earn $30M+!

clues.stem: During the booming 1950s Eisenhower era, how did the TOP U.S. federal marginal income tax rate compare to today’s 37% top rate?
clues.ahaFactoid: From 1954 through 1963, the highest federal income bracket sat at an eye-popping 91% on income above $400,000 for married couples!

clues.stem: Which giant retail-banking brand operates MORE physical brick-and-mortar U.S. bank branches (thousands across every mainland state)?
clues.ahaFactoid: JPMorgan Chase became the first bank operating physical branches across all lower 48 states—while online challengers like Ally and Chime run zero branches!

clues.stem: At typical exchange rates, which major world currency unit buys MORE U.S. dollars per single unit (~$1.25+ USD)?
clues.ahaFactoid: A single British pound sterling consistently buys well over one U.S. dollar—dwarfing single units of yen, pesos, or rupees!

clues.stem: Topping the Fortune 500 revenue table for over a decade straight, which giant rings up MORE annual sales (over $640 billion!) than any other retailer?
clues.ahaFactoid: Founded by Sam Walton in 1962 Rogers, Arkansas, Walmart’s annual revenue tops $640 billion—roughly $1.75 billion ringing through registers every single day!

clues.stem: Storing roughly 2,452 metric tons in Rome vaults, which G7 nation holds MORE official central-bank gold reserves than Japan or the UK?
clues.ahaFactoid: Italy holds the world’s third-largest national gold stockpile behind only the United States and Germany—while Canada famously sold off all its gold bullion!

clues.stem: Raised during the 2008 financial crisis from $100,000, what HIGHER standard insurance limit now protects each depositor per insured U.S. bank?
clues.ahaFactoid: Congress temporarily raised FDIC coverage to $250,000 in October 2008 and made the quarter-million-dollar shield permanent in 2010!

clues.stem: Inside the Federal Reserve’s rate-setting committee (FOMC), how many officials cast regular votes on U.S. interest-rate moves at each meeting?
clues.ahaFactoid: Seven Board Governors, the New York Fed President, and four rotating regional Reserve Bank presidents make up the 12 voting FOMC seats!

clues.stem: When bond prices plunge during an interest-rate spike, what happens to the bond’s current market YIELD—does it move HIGHER or LOWER?
clues.ahaFactoid: Because a bond’s fixed dollar coupon stays constant, paying a lower price for that same stream pushes the effective yield percentage higher!

clues.stem: Stretching from March 2009 until the COVID-19 crash in February 2020, which Wall Street rally lasted LONGER (~11 years!) than any modern bull run?
clues.ahaFactoid: Lasting nearly 131 months without a 20% S&P 500 drop, the post-2009 expansion narrowly outlasted the famous 1990–2000 tech bull market!

clues.stem: Between two 30-year Treasury bonds, which security carries a HIGHER Macaulay duration—making its price swing more violently when interest rates shift?
clues.ahaFactoid: Because a zero-coupon bond pays 100% of its cash at final maturity in Year 30, its Macaulay duration equals the full 30 years!

clues.stem: Three of these Founding Fathers or presidents appear on everyday circulating U.S. coins; spot the Treasury founder who graces the $10 paper bill instead!
clues.ahaFactoid: While Lincoln (1¢), Jefferson (5¢), and FDR (10¢) fill pocket change, first Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton stays strictly on crisp $10 notes!

clues.stem: Three of these famous street spaces appear on a classic Atlantic City Monopoly board; spot the famous New York park that does not!
clues.ahaFactoid: Classic U.S. Monopoly streets all came from Atlantic City, New Jersey—except misspelled "Marven Gardens" in neighboring Margate!

clues.stem: Three of these payment giants operate global card-processing networks; spot the peer-to-peer phone app owned by PayPal!
clues.ahaFactoid: Born in 2009 so roommates could split pizza and rent over texts, Venmo moves cash between bank accounts rather than running a traditional card rail!

clues.stem: Three of these U.S. paper dollar denominations still roll off Treasury presses today; spot the hefty old bill discontinued back in 1969!
clues.ahaFactoid: William McKinley’s $500 bill remains legal tender if you ever find one in an attic—though collectors routinely pay well over $1,000 for it!

clues.stem: Three of these famous red-and-white corporate logos belong to giant American retail or grocery chains; spot the Seattle coffee giant in green!
clues.ahaFactoid: Starbucks switched to its signature forest-green siren apron in 1987 after Howard Schultz merged Il Giornale with the original brown Pike Place logo!

clues.stem: Three of these are tax-advantaged U.S. savings accounts; spot the short-term loan you take out to buy a car!
clues.ahaFactoid: While 401(k)s, Roth IRAs, and 529 plans grow investments with IRS tax perks, an auto loan is consumer debt secured by your vehicle!

clues.stem: Three of these famous brands built their fortunes in consumer tech; spot the 1886 Atlanta beverage icon!
clues.ahaFactoid: Pharmacist John Pemberton brewed Coca-Cola syrup in Atlanta in 1886—over eighty years before Silicon Valley’s Intel launched its first microchip!

clues.stem: Three of these keyboard symbols represent official world currencies; spot the email routing mark!
clues.ahaFactoid: Computer engineer Ray Tomlinson picked the commercial "at" sign in 1971 simply to separate people’s usernames from their host computers!

clues.stem: Three of these common lines appear as tax or benefit deductions on an American paycheck stub; spot the extra cash customers leave on a diner table!
clues.ahaFactoid: Payroll taxes like Social Security (FICA) and Medicare get withheld automatically before payday—whereas diner tips are extra income earned on shift!

clues.stem: Three of these global mega-brands started by selling sneakers and athletic gear; spot the Swedish flat-pack furniture giant!
clues.ahaFactoid: Ingvar Kamprad founded IKEA in 1943 in Sweden—selling pens and wallets by mail before inventing flat-pack bookshelves!

clues.stem: Three of these companies are the big national credit-reporting bureaus behind your credit report; spot the instant bank-transfer network!
clues.ahaFactoid: Owned by major U.S. banks, Zelle moves instant cash between checking accounts—while Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion track credit histories!

clues.stem: Three of these Silicon Valley giants belong to Wall Street’s "Magnificent Seven" mega-cap tech club; spot the Arkansas retail king!
clues.ahaFactoid: Bank of America analyst Michael Hartnett popularized "Magnificent Seven" in 2023 for Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia, Meta, and Tesla!

clues.stem: Three of these powerhouse institutions print or manage national currencies as central banks; spot the private Wall Street asset manager!
clues.ahaFactoid: BlackRock manages trillions in index funds and iShares ETFs for private and pension investors rather than printing national money!

clues.stem: Three of these household icons are owned outright by Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway; spot the rival soft-drink giant he famously avoids!
clues.ahaFactoid: A lifelong Cherry Coke drinker, Warren Buffett has held billions in Coca-Cola stock since 1988 while leaving PepsiCo to rival portfolios!

clues.stem: Three of these European countries adopted the shared Euro currency; spot the Scandinavian nation that kept its own Krona!
clues.ahaFactoid: Swedish voters rejected joining the Eurozone in a 2003 referendum, keeping the colorful Swedish krona alive alongside Denmark and Poland!

clues.stem: Three of these tools belong to Congress and Treasury "fiscal policy"; spot the interest-rate lever controlled independently by the Federal Reserve!
clues.ahaFactoid: Central banks steer monetary policy via interest rates and bond purchases, whereas elected lawmakers wield fiscal policy through taxes and budgets!

clues.stem: Three of these Wall Street phrases describe standard ways to buy or sell shares; spot the IRS tax rule penalizing quick buy-backs of losing stock!
clues.ahaFactoid: Sell a losing stock for a tax write-off and rebuy it within 30 days, and the IRS wash-sale rule blocks your immediate loss deduction!

clues.stem: Three of these U.S. Bankruptcy Code chapters handle individuals or corporations; spot the special chapter reserved strictly for cities and municipalities!
clues.ahaFactoid: Detroit famously filed for Chapter 9 municipal bankruptcy in 2013—while businesses reorganize under Chapter 11 and consumers use Chapters 7 or 13!

clues.stem: Three of these famous economists actually won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences; spot the 1930s British giant who died before it existed!
clues.ahaFactoid: Created by Sweden’s central bank in 1968, the Nobel Economics Prize arrived 22 years after Keynes passed away in 1946!

clues.stem: Three of these Wall Street metrics measure portfolio risk and volatility; spot the macro rule linking falling GDP directly to higher unemployment!
clues.ahaFactoid: Arthur Okun’s 1962 empirical rule tracks national output vs. joblessness—whereas Beta, Sortino, and Value at Risk measure investment volatility!

clues.stem: Three of these classic economics graphs chart wealth distribution or inequality; spot Arthur Laffer’s napkin curve linking tax rates to government revenue!
clues.ahaFactoid: Sketched on a Washington restaurant napkin in 1974, the Laffer curve illustrates tax-rate revenue peaks—while Lorenz, Kuznets, and Pen track inequality!

clues.stem: Three of these 20th-century thinkers anchored the free-market Austrian School of economics; spot the Harvard liberal champion of "The Affluent Society"!
clues.ahaFactoid: John Kenneth Galbraith advised JFK and pushed strong public spending—standing squarely opposite Mises, Hayek, and Rothbard!

clues.stem: On every classic Atlantic City board corner, Monopoly’s cheerful arrow square tells every lucky player: "Collect $200 salary as you pass [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: During the Great Depression, unemployed radiator salesman Charles Darrow kept Monopoly’s $200 "Pass GO" payday high enough to keep players feeling flush!

clues.stem: Debuting in 1997 with two baseball tickets and a hot dog, a famous credit-card ad concluded: "There are some things money can’t buy. For everything else, there’s [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Written by copywriter Joyce King Thomas, Mastercard’s "Priceless" ads ran across more than 100 countries across multiple generations!

clues.stem: Printed boldly across the back of every modern U.S. banknote since 1957, the national motto reads: "In [ _____ ] We Trust."
clues.ahaFactoid: That four-word motto first appeared on U.S. bronze two-cent coins during the Civil War in 1864 before Congress mandated it on paper currency in 1955!

clues.stem: Closing television commercials since 1950 with cupped protective palms, Allstate’s soothing assurance promises: "You’re in good [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Sales executive Davis Ellis coined the comforting slogan after his wife told him their doctor assured her their sick daughter was "in good hands"!

clues.stem: Coined in 1971 by future music legend Barry Manilow as an ad jingle, State Farm’s cozy tagline promises: "Like a good [ _____ ], State Farm is there."
clues.ahaFactoid: Yes—before singing "Copacabana" and "Mandy," Barry Manilow wrote commercial jingles for State Farm, Band-Aid, and KFC!

clues.stem: Inspired unexpectedly by a notorious 1977 last statement, adman Dan Wieden crafted Nike’s crisp three-word global rallying cry: "Just [ _____ ] it."
clues.ahaFactoid: Dan Wieden tweaked death-row prisoner Gary Gilmore’s final words ("Let’s do it") into Nike’s immortal 1988 slogan!

clues.stem: Launching a famous 1985 TV blitz turning down rivals’ cards at upscale spots, Visa’s classic catchphrase boasted: "Visa. It’s [ _____ ] you want to be."
clues.ahaFactoid: The clever campaign spotlighted trendy restaurants and ski resorts that accepted Visa while politely turning away American Express!

clues.stem: With Samuel L. Jackson or Jennifer Garner eyeing the camera, Capital One’s cheeky commercial signature asks: "What’s in your [ _____ ]?"
clues.ahaFactoid: Comedian David Spade and pillaging Visigoth Vikings launched the "What’s in your wallet?" ads back in 2000!

clues.stem: Often paraphrased from Benjamin Franklin’s 1737 "Poor Richard’s Almanack," thrift-minded parents still recite: "A penny saved is a penny [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Franklin originally wrote "A penny saved is twopence clear" in 1737, before later American sayings polished it into "a penny earned"!

clues.stem: Appearing in Benjamin Franklin’s 1748 "Advice to a Young Tradesman," this crisp three-word hustle proverb warns: "Remember that [ _____ ] is money."
clues.ahaFactoid: Franklin argued that idling away half a day costs both the money you didn’t earn AND the cash you spent while loafing!

clues.stem: With a cheerful green gecko leaning on a briefcase, Geico’s long-running radio pitch promises: "15 minutes could save you 15% or more on [ _____ ] insurance."
clues.ahaFactoid: Born during a 1999 actors’ strike when Geico couldn’t hire live spokespeople, the Cockney gecko became one of America’s most recognizable ad mascots!

clues.stem: Whenever Wall Street markets panic and buyers hoard liquid bills over risky shares, traders repeat the blunt three-word maxim: "[ _____ ] is king."
clues.ahaFactoid: Volvo boss Pehr Gyllenhammar popularized "Cash is king" right after the 1987 Black Monday stock crash!

clues.stem: Every rookie investor learns the golden four-word wall-street rule on Day One, even if nerves make it tough: "Buy low, [ _____ ] high."
clues.ahaFactoid: Easy to chant in a bull market—yet behavioral finance shows most panicky humans do the exact opposite during crashes!

clues.stem: Addressing Teldar Paper shareholders in 1987’s "Wall Street," Gordon Gekko declares: "The point is, ladies and gentlemen, that [ _____ ], for lack of a better word, is good."
clues.ahaFactoid: Screenwriter Stanley Weiser based Gekko’s famous speech partly on real 1986 remarks by Wall Street arbitrageur Ivan Boesky—shortly before Boesky went to prison!

clues.stem: Pull the dreaded Chance card with Officer Edgar Mallory pointing sternly at iron bars, and it orders: "Go to Jail. Go directly to Jail. Do not pass GO, do not [ _____ ] $200."
clues.ahaFactoid: Late in a cutthroat Monopoly game, staying IN Jail for three turns is actually smart strategy so you collect rent without landing on hotels!

clues.stem: Distilling contrarian investing into one timeless proverb, Warren Buffett advises shareholders: "Be cautious when others are greedy, and greedy when others are [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Buffett put that mantra into bold action during October 2008, writing a famous New York Times op-ed titled "Buy American. I Am."

clues.stem: Popularized in economics by Milton Friedman after saloonkeepers lured drinkers with free salty snacks, the skeptical maxim warns: "There ain’t no such thing as a free [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Nineteenth-century saloons served salty ham and crackers "free" to paying patrons because the salt guaranteed they’d buy plenty more beer!

clues.stem: Dreamed up in 1947 by Philadelphia copywriter Frances Gerety for De Beers, Advertising Age’s #1 slogan of the 20th century declares: "A diamond is [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Frances Gerety scribbled those four words late at night—and accidentally invented the modern engagement-ring expectation almost single-handedly!

clues.stem: Chiding classical economists who waited passively for markets to heal themselves after slumps, John Maynard Keynes quipped: "In the long run we are all [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Keynes wrote that zinger in his 1923 Tract on Monetary Reform—urging central bankers to calm choppy storms right now rather than wait decades!

clues.stem: Explaining wild daily market swings vs. true business value, Benjamin Graham noted: "In the short run, the market is a voting machine, but in the long run, it is a [ _____ ] machine."
clues.ahaFactoid: Graham taught that exact quote to young Columbia student Warren Buffett, who still cites it to explain meme-stock fads vs. lasting profits!

clues.stem: Warning short-sellers against betting everything on timing a bubble burst, an oft-quoted Wall Street maxim cautions: "Markets can stay irrational longer than you can stay [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Long attributed to Keynes and popularized by strategist Gary Shilling, the warning proved painfully true during both the 1999 dot-com mania and 2021 GameStop!

clues.stem: Calming Europe’s terrifying sovereign-debt panic in July 2012 with three famous words, ECB chief Mario Draghi pledged to preserve the euro: "[ _____ ] it takes."
clues.ahaFactoid: Draghi’s four-word pledge ("Within our mandate, the ECB is ready to do whatever it takes") instantly cooled bond panic without spending a single euro!

clues.stem: Flip over your Visa or Mastercard and check the white signature strip: I’m the secret 3-digit security number websites ask for at checkout. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Standing for Card Verification Value (printed as 4 digits on the front of Amex cards!), I prove you actually hold the physical plastic in hand!

clues.stem: Unlike any other U.S. president, my profile appears on BOTH a circulating coin (facing right in copper) AND a everyday paper banknote ($5). Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Added to the one-cent coin in 1909 to mark his 100th birthday, Lincoln became the first real U.S. president ever pictured on regular American coinage!

clues.stem: Striding across board-game boxes in a tuxedo, white handlebar mustache, and tall black top hat, I’m Parker Brothers’ cheerful cash-flinging mascot. Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Originally named Rich Uncle Pennybags in 1936, cartoonist Dan Fox modeled his jaunty suit after 19th-century financier J.P. Morgan!

clues.stem: Sporting flowing shoulder-length hair on America’s highest regular bill—even though I was never elected U.S. President—I grace the $100 note. Who am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Only two non-presidents appear on modern U.S. bills: Treasury founder Alexander Hamilton ($10) and Founding Father Benjamin Franklin ($100)!

clues.stem: Invented in 1879 by Dayton saloonkeeper James Ritty to stop bartenders from pocketing till money, my loud brass bell earned me the nickname "Incorruptible Cashier." What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Ritty got the idea while watching a ship’s mechanical propeller-revolution counter during a European steamship trip—and John Patterson turned it into NCR!

clues.stem: Printed along the bottom-left corner of every paper check in weird magnetic ink, my nine digits identify which exact U.S. bank holds your account. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Created by the American Bankers Association in 1910, routing transit numbers let automated MICR sorters process millions of paper checks every night!

clues.stem: You must flash my photo-ID membership card at the warehouse door to buy giant 48-packs of paper towels, $4.99 chickens, and $1.50 hot dogs. Which chain am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Co-founder Jim Sinegal famously warned his successor never to raise the $1.50 hot-dog combo price—a promise Costco still honors decades later!

clues.stem: Born out of Confinity and X.com in 1998–2000 so strangers could email cash to eBay sellers, my blue-P payment service became Silicon Valley’s "Mafia." What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Early PayPal founders and engineers went on to launch YouTube, LinkedIn, Yelp, SpaceX, and Palantir across the following decade!

clues.stem: Stand in front of a cash machine and tap four secret numbers into the metal keypad—my inventor originally wanted six digits until his wife overruled him. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Scottish ATM inventor John Shepherd-Barron picked four digits in 1967 because his wife Caroline could only reliably remember four numbers at a time!

clues.stem: Split across Washington’s Board of Governors plus 12 regional banks from Boston to San Francisco, I’m America’s central bank created in 1913. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Signed into law by Woodrow Wilson in 1913 after the Panic of 1907, the Federal Reserve guides U.S. interest rates and banking stability!

clues.stem: Starting in Quincy, Massachusetts in 1950 and later famous for telling America it "Runs on" coffee and glazed rings, which purple-and-orange chain am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Founder Bill Rosenberg initially named his Quincy shop "Open Kettle" in 1948 before rebranding it Dunkin’ Donuts two years later!

clues.stem: Operating facilities in Philadelphia, Denver, San Francisco, and West Point, I’m the Treasury agency that actually strikes every U.S. penny, nickel, dime, and quarter. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: The U.S. Mint strikes every metallic coin in your jar, while the Bureau of Engraving and Printing separately prints all paper dollar bills!

clues.stem: Instead of paying pricey Wall Street stock-pickers to guess winners, I simply buy tiny slices of the entire S&P 500 market at dirt-cheap fees. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: John Bogle launched the first retail index fund at Vanguard in 1975—initially mocked by Wall Street as "Bogle’s Folly" before conquering trillions!

clues.stem: Promise your house or car to a lender as a backup guarantee when borrowing money—if you stop paying, the bank can seize me. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Backing a loan with solid collateral lowers risk for lenders—which is why home mortgages charge far lower interest rates than unsecured credit cards!

clues.stem: Trading outside giant exchanges for under five bucks a share—and hyped in "The Wolf of Wall Street"—I’m a high-risk microcap security. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: While historically priced under $1, the SEC defines any equity trading below $5 per share outside major national exchanges as a "penny stock"!

clues.stem: Borrow money from your broker to buy stocks, and if the shares crash too far, my dreaded phone alert forces you to wire cash fast or get sold out. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Massive margin calls helped turn October 1929’s dip into a cascading meltdown as leveraged speculators dumped shares simultaneously!

clues.stem: Signed by 24 New York brokers under a shady sycamore tree at 68 Wall Street in May 1792, my two-sentence pact laid the foundation for the NYSE. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Signers promised to trade securities only among themselves at a minimum 0.25% commission—establishing Wall Street’s oldest club!

clues.stem: Demonstrated in 1817 using English cloth and Portuguese wine, I’m David Ricardo’s paradox proving both nations profit from trade even if one makes everything faster. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Economists still call Ricardo’s insight one of the least intuitive yet most rock-solid truths in all of social science!

clues.stem: Launched in 1896 and famously weighting 30 giant companies by single-share dollar price instead of total market size, I’m Wall Street’s oldest blue-chip gauge. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Because the Dow adds up share prices of 30 companies and divides by a magic divisor, a $500 stock moves the index ten times more than a $50 giant!

clues.stem: Sketched by a New Zealand economist in 1958 using British wage data, I’m the famous macroeconomic tradeoff curve linking falling unemployment with rising inflation. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: A.W. Phillips also built the MONIAC—a wild 1949 hydraulic computer that pumped colored water through plastic tubes to simulate the British economy!

clues.stem: Flagged by Belgian-American economist Robert Triffin in 1960, I’m the paradox where supplying the world’s reserve currency forces the U.S. to run endless trade deficits. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Triffin warned Congress a full decade early that foreigners holding more dollars than U.S. Fort Knox gold would eventually shatter Bretton Woods—just as happened in 1971!

clues.stem: Published in 1958 with a "whole milk vs. cream" analogy, my Nobel theorem argues that in frictionless markets debt vs. equity leaves a firm’s value unchanged. What am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Franco Modigliani and Merton Miller’s irrelevance theorem launched modern corporate finance by isolating real-world taxes and bankruptcy costs!

clues.stem: Which classic way to handle or track money arrived FIRST in American life?
clues.ahaFactoid: Parker Brothers launched Monopoly in 1935—fifteen years before Diners Club’s cardboard charge card (1950) and decades before ATMs!

clues.stem: Which giant consumer internet brand launched FIRST (debuting online as AuctionWeb on Labor Day weekend 1995)?
clues.ahaFactoid: Pierre Omidyar launched eBay in September 1995—famously selling a broken laser pointer to a collector for $14.83!

clues.stem: Which everyday U.S. president first appeared on a circulating American coin EARLIEST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Victor David Brenner’s Lincoln cent debuted in 1909—twenty-three years ahead of the 1932 Washington quarter and 1938 Jefferson nickel!

clues.stem: Which everyday retail payment milestone arrived MOST RECENTLY for shoppers?
clues.ahaFactoid: IBM’s magnetic stripe arrived in the 1960s, European EMV chips in the 1990s, and Square in 2009—before Apple Pay launched NFC tap-to-pay in October 2014!

clues.stem: Which household retail brand opened its very first store EARLIEST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Rowland Hussey Macy opened his Manhattan dry-goods store in 1858—over a century before Sam Walton opened Walmart #1 in 1962!

clues.stem: Which famous consumer brand went public on the stock market FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: McDonald’s sold IPO shares at $22.50 in April 1965—fifteen years before Nike (1980) and 27 years before Starbucks (1992)!

clues.stem: Which global financial or consumer invention debuted LATER than the others?
clues.ahaFactoid: Satoshi Nakamoto published the nine-page Bitcoin whitepaper in October 2008—years after PayPal (1998), the iPod (2001), and Gmail (2004)!

clues.stem: Which historic U.S. currency or banking landmark came FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: The Continental Congress printed paper "Continentals" in 1775 to fund the Revolutionary War—over a century before the 1913 Federal Reserve!

clues.stem: Which global sportswear business started selling shoes or gear EARLIEST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Adi Dassler formally registered Adidas in Germany in 1949—fifteen years before Phil Knight and Bill Bowerman launched Blue Ribbon Sports (later Nike) in 1964!

clues.stem: Which major credit-card brand launched FIRST (originally as BankAmericard)?
clues.ahaFactoid: Bank of America mailed out 60,000 live BankAmericards to Fresno, California in 1958—eight years before Master Charge (1966) and 27 before Discover (1985)!

clues.stem: Which milestone in American personal finance took effect FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: After the 16th Amendment ratified federal income tax in 1913, the IRS introduced Form 1040 in early 1914—decades before Social Security (1935) or 401(k)s (1978)!

clues.stem: Which infamous Wall Street stock-market plunge happened FIRST in modern history?
clues.ahaFactoid: October 1929 ushered in the Great Depression—nearly six decades before Black Monday (1987) and the 2000 tech crash!

clues.stem: Which major international economic milestone happened MOST RECENTLY?
clues.ahaFactoid: Euro coins and paper banknotes first entered European wallets in January 2002—eight years after NAFTA (1994) and seven after the WTO (1995)!

clues.stem: Which retail investing milestone debuted FIRST for everyday savers?
clues.ahaFactoid: John Bogle’s Vanguard retail index fund opened in 1976—seventeen years before SPDR (SPY) launched America’s first ETF in 1993!

clues.stem: Which major U.S. financial reform law passed Congress EARLIER?
clues.ahaFactoid: Triggered by Enron and WorldCom accounting scandals, Sarbanes-Oxley passed in 2002—eight years before post-2008 Dodd-Frank!

clues.stem: Which world-changing currency shift happened EARLIEST?
clues.ahaFactoid: FDR signed the Gold Reserve Act in January 1934, revaluing gold to $35/oz—ten years before Bretton Woods anchored post-war currencies to the dollar!

clues.stem: Which Nobel-winning quantitative finance breakthrough was published FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Harry Markowitz published Portfolio Selection in 1952—twenty-one years before Black-Scholes priced options and 27 before Kahneman & Tversky!

clues.stem: During the turmoil of 2008–2010, which dramatic financial crisis milestone struck FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: JPMorgan rescued collapsing Bear Stearns for $2 a share in March 2008—six full months before Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy in September!

clues.stem: Which global banking-plumbing breakthrough went live FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Barclays installed the world’s first cash-dispensing ATM in Enfield, North London in June 1967—six years before banks founded SWIFT in Brussels!

clues.stem: Which foundational economics treatise was published EARLIEST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Irish-French banker Richard Cantillon’s 1755 essay pioneered circular-flow economics—predating Adam Smith, Thomas Malthus, and David Ricardo!

clues.stem: Which infamous financial blowup shook markets FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Bad interest-rate derivative bets pushed California’s Orange County into a $1.6 billion municipal bankruptcy in December 1994—America’s biggest then!

clues.stem: Which foundational institution of global capitalism emerged FIRST?
clues.ahaFactoid: Venice’s state-backed grain and bond exchange in the 1150s predated the Medici Bank (1397), the Amsterdam Stock Exchange (1602), and Bank of England (1694)!

clues.stem: Introduced in 1932 to honor the bicentennial of his birth, which founding president has graced the front of the U.S. quarter ever since?
clues.ahaFactoid: Originally meant as a one-year commemorative coin in 1932, John Flanagan’s Washington portrait proved so popular it stayed permanently!

clues.stem: Since 1965, U.S. quarters and dimes stopped using pure silver and switched to a shiny cupronickel outer sandwich bonded over what reddish core metal?
clues.ahaFactoid: Flip any modern U.S. quarter onto its thin edge and you can clearly spot that reddish strip of pure copper sandwiched inside!

clues.stem: Added alongside the thimble and iron in early 1950s editions, which loyal four-legged Monopoly metal token consistently polls as players’ #1 favorite?
clues.ahaFactoid: Hasbro’s fan polls repeatedly crowned the Scottie Dog #1—even surviving votes that briefly retired the iron and thimble!

clues.stem: Issued by Abraham Lincoln’s Treasury in 1861 to finance the Civil War, demand notes earned the lasting nickname "greenbacks" simply because of what anti-theft trick?
clues.ahaFactoid: At the time, green ink was harder to photograph and forge with primitive 1860s black-and-white cameras—giving U.S. cash its signature hue!

clues.stem: In 1901, financier J.P. Morgan merged Andrew Carnegie’s mills with rivals to create the world’s first billion-dollar corporation—named what?
clues.ahaFactoid: Valued at $1.4 billion on opening day in 1901, U.S. Steel alone produced two-thirds of all steel poured in the United States!

clues.stem: Aside from narrow hardship exceptions, tapping your regular 401(k) retirement stash before age 59½ triggers what automatic IRS extra penalty on top of income tax?
clues.ahaFactoid: Congress built that flat 10% early-withdrawal surcharge to nudge workers into leaving retirement compounding untouched until their golden years!

clues.stem: Paid just $35 in 1971 while studying graphic design at Portland State, Carolyn Davidson sketched what iconic wing-inspired sports logo?
clues.ahaFactoid: Phil Knight initially sighed "I don’t love it," then twelve years later surprised Davidson with a gold Swoosh ring and Nike stock worth millions!

clues.stem: On October 19, 1987, computerized portfolio-insurance sell programs triggered Wall Street’s steepest single-day percentage crash ever—falling how far on the Dow?
clues.ahaFactoid: The Dow shed 508 points in one terrifying Monday—prompting regulators to install automatic market-halting "circuit breakers" still used today!

clues.stem: Born inside a bustling 1688 Tower Street coffeehouse where ship captains traded maritime shipping news, which legendary British insurance marketplace bears its owner’s name?
clues.ahaFactoid: Underwriters at Lloyd’s of London still ring the salvaged HMS Lutine ship’s bell inside the underwriting room for solemn maritime announcements!

clues.stem: Developed independently by Robert Mundell and Marcus Fleming, the "Macroeconomic Trilemma" says a nation cannot keep free capital flow, a fixed exchange rate, and what third tool?
clues.ahaFactoid: Pick any two of the three corners: the U.S. keeps independent Fed interest rates and open capital, so the dollar must float freely against foreign currencies!

clues.stem: Treasury Portrait Desk: Currently appearing on the front of the U.S. $50 bill beside the U.S. Capitol building on the reverse is Civil War general [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: Grant’s portrait has graced the $50 bill continuously since 1914—and modern $50 notes sport pink-and-blue anti-counterfeit shading!

clues.stem: Burbank Deal Wire, 2006: Paying $7.4 billion in stock, [ _____ ] acquired Pixar Animation Studios—putting Steve Jobs on its board of directors.
clues.ahaFactoid: That 2006 deal launched a legendary acquisition streak adding Marvel (2009), Lucasfilm (2012), and 21st Century Fox (2019) under the Mouse House roof!

clues.stem: Retail Wire, 1962: Wanting an upscale discount store distinct from parent Dayton’s in Minnesota, executives launched [ _____ ] with a bright red bullseye.
clues.ahaFactoid: In an uncanny twist of 1962 retail history, Walmart, Kmart, Target, and Kohl’s ALL opened their very first discount stores in the same single year!

clues.stem: Chicago Business Wire, 1955: Amazed that two California brothers bought eight of his Multimixer milkshake machines, salesman [ _____ ] franchised McDonald’s nationwide.
clues.ahaFactoid: Ray Kroc bought out Richard and Maurice McDonald for $2.7 million in 1961—turning real-estate leases to franchisees into a fast-food empire!

clues.stem: Omaha Dispatch, 1965: Buying up a struggling New England [ _____ ] mill out of spite over a tiny nickel price cut, Warren Buffett kept its name for his holding empire.
clues.ahaFactoid: Buffett later joked that buying the dying Berkshire Hathaway shirt-lining mill was one of his worst investments—until he turned its shell into a trillion-dollar giant!

clues.stem: Chicago Retail Wire, 1986: Airing during Super Bowl XX, Sears shook up credit cards by launching [ _____ ] with zero annual fee and cash-back rewards.
clues.ahaFactoid: Competitors laughed at Sears’s 1% "Cashback Bonus" in 1986—yet cash-back rewards quickly became the single biggest perk in American credit cards!

clues.stem: Monetary Dispatch, 1945: Created at Bretton Woods alongside the IMF to fund post-war rebuilding and global development loans, the [ _____ ] opened in Washington.
clues.ahaFactoid: Officially the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the World Bank’s very first loan went to France in 1947 ($250 million)!

clues.stem: Boston Wire, 1977–1990: Averaging an astonishing 29.2% annual return while urging everyday shoppers to "invest in what you know," [ _____ ] led Fidelity’s Magellan Fund.
clues.ahaFactoid: Peter Lynch spotted blockbuster stocks like Dunkin’ Donuts and Hanes simply by noticing what his wife and daughters raved about at the mall!

clues.stem: Washington Wire, 2010: Named after a towering former Fed chief, the [ _____ ] Rule barred commercial banks from making risky proprietary trading bets with customer deposits.
clues.ahaFactoid: Standing 6-foot-7 with a fondness for cheap cigars, Paul Volcker had previously conquered 1970s inflation by hiking Fed rates near 20%!

clues.stem: Monetary Wire, 1930: Showing why lenders demand higher bond coupons whenever prices climb, Yale economist [ _____ ] linked nominal rates to real returns plus expected inflation.
clues.ahaFactoid: Though famous for his Fisher Equation, Irving Fisher sadly wrecked his own fortune by insisting stocks stood at a "permanently high plateau" days before the 1929 crash!

clues.stem: Perched atop an unfinished 13-step stone pyramid on the reverse of every U.S. $1 bill, a glowing triangle holds what watchful detail?
clues.ahaFactoid: Chosen in 1782 for the Great Seal of the United States, the Eye of Providence symbolizes divine watchfulness over the young republic’s 13 colonies!

clues.stem: Wearing a black morning coat, white mustache, and tall top hat while leaning on a cane—what real-life Monopoly mascot detail sits smoothly atop his upper lip?
clues.ahaFactoid: Notice the Mandela Effect: Rich Uncle Pennybags wears NO monocle (Mr. Peanut has the monocle!)—his bold bushy white mustache defines his cheerful grin!

clues.stem: Flip a modern U.S. five-cent nickel over to its reverse side, and Thomas Jefferson’s Virginia brick estate stands front and center—what is it called?
clues.ahaFactoid: Architect Felix Schlag won $1,000 in a 1938 Treasury contest for that clean Monticello facade—before Jefferson’s portrait shifted to a forward gaze in 2006!

clues.stem: Four bold cobalt-blue wedges spinning tightly around an open white square inside an octagon—which Wall Street banking giant has used this geometric emblem since 1961?
clues.ahaFactoid: Designed by Chermayeff & Geismar in 1961, Chase’s blue octagon became one of America’s earliest purely abstract corporate logos—no letters required!

clues.stem: Flip open a crisp, rarely spent U.S. $2 bill to its back engraving, and John Trumbull’s sweeping painting shows the 1776 drafting of what document?
clues.ahaFactoid: Introduced for the 1976 U.S. Bicentennial, the $2 reverse faithfully adapts John Trumbull’s famous Capitol rotunda painting!

clues.stem: Nostrils flared and tail lashed high in 7,100 pounds of gleaming bronze near Bowling Green, Arturo Di Modica secretly dropped what guerilla sculpture in 1989?
clues.ahaFactoid: Di Modica spent $360,000 of his own savings building the Charging Bull after the 1987 crash and unloaded it off a flatbed truck in five minutes at 1 a.m.!

clues.stem: Struck in 1979 with an eleven-sided inner rim and an eagle landing on the Moon on the reverse, which American suffragist debuted on a circulating U.S. coin?
clues.ahaFactoid: Sadly, shoppers confused the 1979 Susan B. Anthony dollar constantly with quarters because both coins had nearly identical size and silver edges!

clues.stem: Woven directly through the front of modern U.S. $100 notes, a wide cobalt-blue vertical strip makes tiny Liberty Bells flip into "100"s as you tilt it. What is it?
clues.ahaFactoid: Hundreds of thousands of microscopic lenses embedded inside the blue 3D ribbon create real optical motion—making home scanning impossible!

clues.stem: Crafted from polished white whelk and purple quahog clam shells strung carefully into ceremonial belts, what prized medium served across Northeastern Indigenous trade?
clues.ahaFactoid: Early New England colonists ran so short on British silver coins that Connecticut and Massachusetts formally accepted wampum beads as legal tender into the 1660s!

clues.stem: Printed on velvet, leather, porcelain, and playing cards during Weimar Germany’s 1920s hyperinflation when regular marks hit trillions, what emergency town money appeared?
clues.ahaFactoid: Meaning literally "necessity money," colorful local Notgeld issues became prized collector art across German municipalities during post-WWI cash shortages!

clues.stem: Mint Klaxon! Three of these facts about U.S. paper currency are 100% genuine Treasury specs, while one common assumption fails the lab test. Spot the myth!
choices: Bills are pressed from tree wood
Tiny red and blue fibers live inside
clues.ahaFactoid: U.S. dollar bills contain ZERO wood pulp—their 75% cotton and 25% linen blend keeps them crisp even after surviving a washing machine!

clues.stem: Credit Klaxon! Three of these U.S. credit-score guidelines are true consumer rules, while one scary rumor stops people from checking their finances. Spot the myth!
clues.ahaFactoid: Pulling your own credit report or FICO score counts as a harmless "soft inquiry" and never deducts even a single point!

clues.stem: Pocket Change Klaxon! Three of these U.S. coin facts are true, while one popular claim about the 1-cent coin’s value is upside down. Spot the myth!
choices: Pennies cost under half a cent
Nickels also cost over face value
clues.ahaFactoid: Each U.S. penny actually costs the Mint over 3 cents to make and ship—and every nickel costs over 11 cents!

clues.stem: Board Game Klaxon! Three of these Monopoly rules appear in Parker Brothers’ official instruction sheet, while one beloved family house rule is completely made up. Spot the myth!
choices: You collect rent while in Jail
Free Parking pays out tax fines
clues.ahaFactoid: Official Monopoly rules insist Free Parking does absolutely NOTHING—dumping tax fines into the center just makes games drag on for hours!

clues.stem: Wallet Klaxon! Three of these banking and card facts are true U.S. law, while one assumption about ATM habits or bills is wrong. Spot the myth!
clues.ahaFactoid: Even though U.S. cash is legal tender for debts, private coffee shops and buses face zero federal law forcing them to take cash or $100 bills upfront!

clues.stem: Paycheck Klaxon! Three of these U.S. tax realities are completely accurate, while one fearful office-breakroom myth fools workers every April. Spot the myth!
choices: Capital gains rates vary by hold
A raise can cut net pay via bracket
clues.ahaFactoid: Because U.S. tax brackets are marginal, a higher rate applies ONLY to the extra dollars above the threshold—a raise never makes your whole paycheck shrink!

clues.stem: Bank Vault Klaxon! Three of these federal deposit rules are real protection, while one common misunderstanding leaves rookie investors exposed. Spot the myth!
clues.ahaFactoid: FDIC insurance shields checking, savings, and CDs if an insured bank fails—never stock, bond, or crypto market losses!

clues.stem: Currency Klaxon! Three of these U.S. monetary facts are true today, while one widely believed myth ended back in 1971. Spot the myth!
choices: Fort Knox gold backs each $1 bill
Dollars run as fiat legal tender
clues.ahaFactoid: Richard Nixon severed the dollar’s final link to gold in August 1971—today U.S. currency is backed by the "full faith and credit" of the U.S. economy!

clues.stem: Wall Street Klaxon! Three of these 1929 Great Crash facts are solidly documented history, while one lurid newspaper cliché is wildly exaggerated. Spot the myth!
clues.ahaFactoid: John Kenneth Galbraith showed Wall Street’s suicide rate stayed flat in late 1929—most "leaping broker" tales began as dark gallows jokes!

clues.stem: Econ Classics Klaxon! Three of these facts about Adam Smith’s 1776 "Wealth of Nations" are true, while one assumption about its most famous phrase is false. Spot the myth!
choices: He began with a pin-factory case
clues.ahaFactoid: Shocking but true: Adam Smith’s famous phrase "invisible hand" appears only ONCE in the entire 900-page Wealth of Nations (and once in Theory of Moral Sentiments)!

clues.stem: Central-bank animal showdown: which Federal Reserve nickname describes officials eager to HIKE interest rates to cool inflation?
clues.ahaFactoid: Hawks prioritize fighting inflation with tighter money, whereas policy doves favor lower rates to spur hiring and borrowing!

clues.stem: Checkout counter showdown: swipe which rectangular card and money leaves your own checking account almost immediately rather than adding to a monthly bill?
clues.ahaFactoid: Debit cards pull directly from funds you already hold in checking—whereas credit cards represent a short-term loan settled at month’s end!

clues.stem: Personal balance-sheet split: in simple accounting terms, is an unpaid $25,000 student loan on your ledger an Asset or a Liability?
clues.ahaFactoid: Assets put money or value in your pocket (cash, home equity, stocks), while Liabilities represent debts you owe to others!

clues.stem: Payday envelope split: what do accountants call your BIGGER starting salary number BEFORE federal taxes and health insurance get subtracted?
clues.ahaFactoid: Think of a big grocery "gross" total first—then taxes and deductions shrink it down to the "net" cash you actually carry home!

clues.stem: Stock-chart split: when a pricey $300 share executes a 3-for-1 split into three $100 shares, what happens to your total dollar investment value?
clues.ahaFactoid: Slicing one $300 pizza into three $100 thirds leaves the exact same amount of pizza—it simply makes single shares cheaper for smaller buyers!

clues.stem: Macro price showdown: if inflation cools from 8% down to 3%, prices are still rising more slowly rather than actually falling—what do economists call that slowdown?
clues.ahaFactoid: Disinflation means the car is still moving forward, just easing off the gas—whereas deflation means putting prices into reverse!

clues.stem: Options-desk showdown: which Wall Street contract gives buyers the right to SELL shares at a locked-in floor price if the market drops?
clues.ahaFactoid: Think "put it away" on a shelf: a Put grants the right to sell at a set strike price, while a Call grants the right to buy!

clues.stem: Wall Street trading split: when shares change hands between regular investors on the NYSE years after an IPO, which market does that daily trading happen in?
clues.ahaFactoid: Companies raise fresh cash only once in the Primary market (like an IPO)—everything you trade afterward on your brokerage app is Secondary market trading!

clues.stem: National scorecard split: which version of Gross Domestic Product strips out rising prices so economists can measure genuine output growth across decades?
clues.ahaFactoid: Adjusting raw Nominal GDP into inflation-cleaned Real GDP stops rising grocery and gas prices from disguising stagnant production!

clues.stem: Information-economics split: if only high-risk buyers rush to grab flat-rate insurance before insurers know their medical history, which pre-contract trap hits the pool?
clues.ahaFactoid: Pioneered by George Akerlof’s "Market for Lemons," adverse selection occurs BEFORE signing when hidden info skews who buys in!

clues.stem: Walk up to a U.S. Costco food court vs. a corner store cooler: which beloved inflation-proof bargain costs MORE ($1.50 vs. 99 cents)?
clues.ahaFactoid: Costco’s quarter-pound hot dog and soda have stayed locked at $1.50 since 1985, while AriZona’s big tallboy tea has stayed 99 cents since 1992!

clues.stem: Unbox classic home video-game consoles on launch day: which Sony or Nintendo system debuted at a HIGHER U.S. retail price ($499.99 disc edition)?
clues.ahaFactoid: Sony’s disc-drive PS5 launched at $499.99 in 2020—double Nintendo’s $249.99 Wii (2006) and well above the $299.99 Switch (2017)!

clues.stem: Step up to an average U.S. movie-theater box office in 1966 vs. 1996: which ticket actually cost MORE than a dollar ($1.09 average)?
clues.ahaFactoid: Average U.S. movie tickets climbed past $1.00 for the first time right around 1965–66 ($1.09)—compared to roughly 23 cents in 1933 and 53 cents in 1950!

clues.stem: Play "The Price Is Right" in the supermarket produce and meat aisles: which grocery staple averages a HIGHER U.S. price per pound?
clues.ahaFactoid: Bananas remain America’s cheapest fresh fruit (hovering near 60¢/lb for decades!), whereas ribeye beef routinely runs $12–$18+ per pound!

clues.stem: Grab a 2007 Apple launch receipt: which pocket device debuted at a HIGHER starting U.S. retail price ($499 for the 4GB model)?
clues.ahaFactoid: Steve Jobs unveiled the first iPhone at $499 (4GB) and $599 (8GB) with a two-year contract—quickly dropping the 8GB model to $399 months later!

clues.stem: Drop a birthday card in a blue U.S. mailbox today: which postage rate costs MORE than 70 cents for a single first-class ounce?
clues.ahaFactoid: First-class stamps cost 22¢ in 1985, 32¢ in 1995, and 37¢ in 2005—before climbing above 70¢ in 2024!

clues.stem: Peek at massive adult-collector Lego sets: which giant 7,541-piece Star Wars kit carries a HIGHER original shelf price ($849.99)?
clues.ahaFactoid: At 7,541 bricks and nearly 30 pounds boxed, Lego’s Ultimate Collector Series Millennium Falcon ranks among the priciest retail Lego sets ever sold!

clues.stem: Pull up to America’s oldest fast-food burger chain in 1921 Wichita: how cheap was a single original White Castle slider back then?
clues.ahaFactoid: White Castle sold square steam-grilled sliders for a nickel from 1921 clear into the late 1940s—giving birth to the iconic "Buy ’Em by the Sack!" slogan!

clues.stem: Toss classic baking staples into a grocery cart: which dairy item almost always costs MORE per pound at U.S. supermarkets?
clues.ahaFactoid: A pound of real butter typically runs $4–$6, easily topping a pound of white sugar, flour, or iodized salt (~$1 or less per pound)!

clues.stem: Compare ticket stubs at Anaheim’s front gate: how much MORE expensive is a standard 1-day Disneyland adult ticket today (~$104–$206) vs. opening day in 1955 ($1)?
clues.ahaFactoid: Opening-day Disneyland charged $1.00 admission plus individual ride coupons (10¢ to 35¢)—meaning a full day of rides cost around $3.50 in 1955!

clues.stem: Order bulk bakery supplies by traditional quantity: which count packs MORE eggs into the delivery crate?
clues.ahaFactoid: Twelve dozens make one full gross (144 items)—while a baker’s dozen adds one extra loaf (13) to guard against underweight penalties!

clues.stem: Adjusting 1959’s original $3.00 Mattel Barbie doll for U.S. inflation (~$32 today), how does a basic modern fashionista Barbie shelf price (~$10–$12) compare?
clues.ahaFactoid: Thanks to global scale and molded plastics, a basic $11 Barbie today actually costs roughly one-third of her inflation-adjusted 1959 launch price!

clues.stem: Flash back to late 1998 U.S. averages: which liquid sold for MORE per gallon across most American towns—regular unleaded gasoline (~$1.05) or whole milk (~$2.70)?
clues.ahaFactoid: During 1998–99’s oil glut, U.S. regular gasoline dipped under $1.00 a gallon in dozens of states—less than half the price of milk!

clues.stem: Buy a 30-second Super Bowl commercial: how does a ~$7 million modern slot compare to Super Bowl I in 1967 (~$42,000)?
clues.ahaFactoid: A 30-second Super Bowl spot climbed from ~$42,000 in 1967 past $1 million in 1995 and ~$7–$8 million today!

clues.stem: Compare Nintendo’s classic 1980s U.S. launch tags: which box carried the HIGHER retail sticker?
clues.ahaFactoid: Nintendo’s 1985 U.S. Deluxe Set launched near $179.99 (with R.O.B. and Duck Hunt), nearly double the pocket Game Boy’s $89.95 debut in 1989!

clues.stem: On Ray Kroc’s 1955 Illinois menu board, regular hamburgers cost 15 cents and fries cost 10 cents—which classic menu item actually cost MORE (20 cents)?
clues.ahaFactoid: In 1955 McDonald’s charged 15¢ for a hamburger, 19¢ for a cheeseburger, 10¢ for fries or coffee, and 20¢ for a creamy milkshake!

clues.stem: Browse the supermarket spice rack: by weight per ounce, which baking spice consistently ranks FAR MORE expensive than black pepper, cinnamon, or cloves?
clues.ahaFactoid: Labor-intensive hand-pollination of orchid blossoms in Madagascar pushes genuine vanilla beans behind only saffron as the world’s priciest spice!

clues.stem: Since 1980, average U.S. undergraduate college tuition and fees rose at roughly what pace compared to overall consumer inflation (CPI)?
clues.ahaFactoid: While overall U.S. consumer prices roughly tripled since 1980, average public and private college tuition soared well over six-to-tenfold!

clues.stem: Order big-ticket American dreams from 1925 mail catalogs: which Sears or Ford purchase carried a HIGHER price tag ($1,500–$3,500 vs. $260)?
clues.ahaFactoid: Between 1908 and 1940, Sears sold over 70,000 mail-order "Honor Bilt" kit houses shipped by boxcar with pre-cut lumber and blueprints!

clues.stem: At traditional U.S. movie-theater concession stands, which snack carries a HIGHER raw percentage gross profit margin (~90%+) than boxed candy?
clues.ahaFactoid: Pennies of fountain syrup mixed with tap water top even theater popcorn’s famous ~85% margin—and easily crush boxed candy (~45%–50%)!

clues.stem: Before the 1886 Hall-Heroult smelting breakthrough made soda cans cheap, which shiny metal was actually MORE expensive per ounce than pure gold—capping the Washington Monument?
clues.ahaFactoid: Napoleon III famously served honored royal guests on aluminum plates while lesser nobles had to settle for plain gold dinnerware!

clues.stem: When RCA launched America’s first mass-market color television (the CT-100) in 1954 at $1,000, how did its price compare to a typical new budget car (~$1,700)?
clues.ahaFactoid: At $1,000 (~$11,500+ today) for a tiny 12-inch round screen, RCA sold barely 5,000 CT-100 color sets before color TV finally took off in the mid-1960s!

clues.stem: Three of these everyday items sit on standard U.S. supermarket shelves; spot the rubber product sold at auto-service shops instead!
clues.ahaFactoid: Supermarket pricing baskets track pantry staples like soup, cereal, and macaroni—leaving Goodyear and Michelin radial tires for the garage!

clues.stem: Three of these famous dollar-menu deals come from American drive-thru chains; spot the Swedish furniture store famous for $1 hot dogs and meatballs!
clues.ahaFactoid: IKEA runs its ultra-cheap restaurant as a classic retail "loss leader" so weary shoppers stay inside the store longer rather than leaving hungry!

clues.stem: Three of these classic pricing games appear on "The Price Is Right"; spot the quiz round where contestants bet on "Daily Doubles"!
clues.ahaFactoid: Daily Double belongs to Jeopardy!—while Plinko, Cliff Hangers (with the yodeling mountain climber!), and the Big Wheel Showcase Showdown rule CBS mornings!

clues.stem: Three of these holiday shopping crazes sold out toy-store shelves in the 1990s; spot the 2020 video-game console!
clues.ahaFactoid: While Elmo (1996), Tamagotchi (1997), and Furby (1998) sparked 1990s mall sprints, Microsoft’s Xbox Series X launched in November 2020!

clues.stem: Three of these stores charge an annual membership fee to shop bulk pallets; spot the corner pharmacy you can walk right into for free!
clues.ahaFactoid: Warehouse clubs keep product markups ultra-slim (~14% max at Costco) because annual membership cards provide the steady core profit!

clues.stem: Three of these surprise add-on fees hit travelers when booking budget airline tickets; spot the pricey snack fridge sitting inside a hotel room!
