clues.stem: Detroit Labor Wire, 1914: Doubling assembly-line pay overnight to a shocking [ _____ ] daily wage, Henry Ford slashed turnover so workers could actually afford his cars.
clues.ahaFactoid: Ford’s $5-a-day announcement drew 10,000 job seekers outside Highland Park’s gates the very next morning—and halved costly worker turnover!

clues.stem: Economics Wire, 1929: Showing why two equal-price ice-cream carts park back-to-back in the middle of a beach, Harold [ _____ ] explained brand clustering.
clues.ahaFactoid: Hotelling’s Law explains why rival pharmacies, burger joints, and gas stations cluster right across the street from each other at busy corners!

clues.stem: Swiveling smoothly toward you on a white coffee-shop counter after handing over a $5 muffin, three glowing boxes offer 18%, 20%, and 25% gratuity buttons:
clues.ahaFactoid: Tablet point-of-sale prompts turned quick counter orders into automatic tip decisions—coining the phrase "tipflation" across cafes nationwide!

clues.stem: Wearing tiny green lederhosen on a painted Alps track, a cheerful miniature figure steps upward one dollar-error notch at a time until risking a cliff plunge:
clues.ahaFactoid: Named Hans on set, the little cardboard mountaineer stops safely on the ledge as long as total pricing guesses miss by $25 or less!

clues.stem: Stamped over an original price with bold red numerals reading "WAS $24.99 / NOW $12.48" and a crisp percentage badge beside a bright red bullseye:
clues.ahaFactoid: Notice savvy Target shoppers look at the tiny corner percentage—30%, 50%, or 70% off—to predict when the next weekly clearance drop arrives!

clues.stem: Inserted into a shiny chrome slot on a grocery cart handle to release a short metal chain—and returned right back to your palm when you park the cart:
clues.ahaFactoid: Aldi’s 25-cent cart deposit lets stores skip hiring lot attendants—passing the saved labor straight into lower milk and egg prices!

clues.stem: Placed squarely at 36-inch toddler eye level along a colorful grocery aisle, bright cartoon mascots stare straight out at kids in shopping-cart seats:
clues.ahaFactoid: Cornell researchers found cartoon cereal mascots are deliberately angled downward to lock eyes directly with kids sitting inside shopping carts!

clues.stem: Spotted quietly in the upper-right corner of a white warehouse price sign ending in ".97"—a tiny printed star warning bargain hunters this item won’t be restocked:
clues.ahaFactoid: Seasoned Costco shoppers call that tiny corner asterisk the "Death Star"—signaling a final clearance markdown before the product vanishes!

clues.stem: Laid across a sandwich counter next to a yellow tape measure in a viral 2013 Australian photo, an 11-inch sub sparked class-action lawsuits over what famous label?
clues.ahaFactoid: Subway eventually settled and stepped up oven-dough uniformity audits after that viral ruler photo exposed uneven 11-inch loaves!

clues.stem: Resting snugly on wood excelsior inside a miniature air-holed cardboard pet carrier, Gary Dahl sold 1.5 million smooth Mexican beach stones in 1975 for $3.95 apiece:
clues.ahaFactoid: Gary Dahl came up with the $3.95 Pet Rock gag in a Los Gatos bar—including a hilarious 32-page owner’s manual teaching the rock to "sit" and "stay"!

clues.stem: Sealed inside tamper-proof blue assay plastic and stamped "999.9 FINE GOLD 1 OZ," Costco stunned shoppers by selling millions of dollars of these shiny bullion bars:
clues.ahaFactoid: Costco’s 1-ounce PAMP Suisse Lady Fortuna gold bars routinely sell out online within hours—especially for 2% Executive Cashback members!

clues.stem: Wrapped in a crisp white satin ribbon over trademarked Pantone 1837 robin’s-egg-blue cardboard—Charles Lewis Tiffany famously refused to sell the empty box at ANY price:
clues.ahaFactoid: In 1906, the New York Sun wrote that Charles Tiffany had one rule: "Money cannot buy a Tiffany box—it comes only with a purchase inside!"

clues.stem: Concession Klaxon! Three of these wild movie-theater pricing realities are 100% true industry economics, while one common complaint about studios is backwards. Spot the myth!
choices: Large tubs cost pennies extra corn
clues.ahaFactoid: Studios routinely claim 55%–65%+ of opening-weekend ticket revenue, leaving movie theaters dependent on high-margin popcorn and fountain drinks!

clues.stem: Travel Deal Klaxon! Three of these airfare pricing rules are true today, while one classic midnight internet hack has been debunked by booking data. Spot the myth!
clues.ahaFactoid: Expedia and ARC booking data show airfare algorithms reprice continuously all week—Sunday bookings actually nudge ahead of Tuesday on many routes!

clues.stem: Retail History Klaxon! Three of these Black Friday facts are genuine, while the feel-good PR origin story stores love repeating gets history backwards. Spot the myth!
clues.ahaFactoid: Philadelphia traffic officers coined "Black Friday" in the 1950s–60s to dread post-Thanksgiving gridlock and shoplifting—not accounting ink!

clues.stem: Gas Pump Klaxon! Three of these U.S. fuel-station pricing quirks are 100% real, while one costly pump habit wastes drivers’ money. Spot the myth!
choices: Premium gas boosts all car mileage
Prices end in 9/10ths of a cent
Summer blends cost more to refine
clues.ahaFactoid: Putting pricey 91–93 octane fuel into a standard 87-octane car adds zero extra power or mileage unless your engine specifically requires premium!

clues.stem: Browser Tab Klaxon! Three of these online travel pricing facts are real, while one stubborn traveler superstition rarely changes posted fares. Spot the myth!
choices: Fare buckets jump as seats sell out
clues.ahaFactoid: Airline fare hikes happen when the last discounted fare bucket sells out across the reservation system—not because of your browser cookies!

clues.stem: Car Lot Klaxon! Three of these auto-dealership pricing realities are true U.S. rules, while one common buyer assumption about window stickers is false. Spot the myth!
choices: Popular SUVs can sell above MSRP
clues.ahaFactoid: MSRP stands for Manufacturer’s SUGGESTED Retail Price—during 2021–22 chip shortages, dealers legally added thousands in "market adjustments" above it!

clues.stem: Warehouse Klaxon! Three of these Costco pricing truths are documented corporate history, while one claim about how the chain makes profit is upside down. Spot the myth!
choices: Costco earns most profit on hot dogs
clues.ahaFactoid: Costco sells $1.50 hot dogs and $4.99 rotisserie chickens near or below cost—earning the lion’s share of its net income directly from annual membership fees!

clues.stem: Checkout Tax Klaxon! Three of these U.S. sales-tax facts are true state law, while one broad generalization fails five counterexamples. Spot the myth!
choices: Oregon also skips statewide sales tax
Every U.S. state levies sales tax
Delaware charges zero state sales tax
City taxes often stack atop states
clues.ahaFactoid: Five U.S. states—Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire, and Oregon—charge zero statewide sales tax at checkout!

clues.stem: Outlet Mall Klaxon! Three of these outlet-center pricing truths are documented retail practice, while one dreamy shopper assumption is largely outdated. Spot the myth!
choices: All outlet stock is boutique surplus
Tanger and Simon anchor outlet malls
clues.ahaFactoid: Today, roughly 80%+ of goods in outlet malls are "made-for-outlet" garments sewn specifically with lighter fabric or simpler stitching—not leftover flagship items!

clues.stem: Luxury History Klaxon! Three of these high-end auction and retail facts are real history, while one romanticized claim about Faberge or porcelain fails inspection. Spot the myth!
choices: Tsars gifted Faberge eggs at Easter
Each Faberge egg sold at $10 retail
clues.ahaFactoid: Imperial Faberge Easter eggs were priceless bespoke royal commissions crafted over a full year—never stocked on $10 retail shelves!

clues.stem: Storefront ledger showdown: which price tier represents the LOWER bulk rate a manufacturer charges a store owner before shoppers buy single items off the shelf?
clues.ahaFactoid: Stores buy pallets at lower Wholesale prices and mark them up to Retail prices to cover rent, staff wages, and lighting!

clues.stem: Supermarket aisle split: which lower-priced cereal or medicine box is often made in comparable factories without costly national TV ad campaigns?
clues.ahaFactoid: Retailers like Costco (Kirkland Signature) and Trader Joe’s sell private-label staples up to 30% cheaper by skipping national ad budgets!

clues.stem: Pizzeria budget split: is the monthly brick-oven shop rent you pay whether you sell ten pies or ten thousand pies a Fixed Cost or a Variable Cost?
clues.ahaFactoid: Shop rent stays flat regardless of pizza volume (Fixed), whereas cheese, pepperoni, and cardboard boxes climb with every order (Variable)!

clues.stem: Coupon math showdown: on a $100 jacket, which markdown leaves you paying LESS at the register—one clean 50% off coupon, or two stacked 25% off discounts?
clues.ahaFactoid: Taking 25% off $100 drops it to $75, and taking another 25% off $75 leaves $56.25—so one bold 50% off beats two stacked 25% coupons every time!

clues.stem: Economist elasticity split: when a lifesaving drug or daily commuter bridge toll jumps 30% and buyers still have to pay it, economists call that demand what?
clues.ahaFactoid: Demand is inelastic when price hikes barely dent purchases (insulin, tap water), whereas movie tickets and restaurant meals are elastic—shoppers easily skip them!

clues.stem: Ticket-stub showdown: why does 1939’s "Gone with the Wind" ($0.23 tickets) still top "Avatar" ($12+ tickets) ONLY when economists adjust box-office grosses for inflation?
clues.ahaFactoid: Comparing raw 1939 quarters against 2020s $15 IMAX tickets ignores decades of rising prices—inflation-adjusted "real dollars" reveal true tickets sold!

clues.stem: Flower-market showdown: at Aalsmeer’s giant Dutch tulip auction, does the big wall clock tick prices UPWARD from a low bid or count prices DOWNWARD until a buyer buzzes?
clues.ahaFactoid: Dutch auctions start sky-high and drop every fraction of a second—forcing florists to smash the button the instant value beats rival buyers!

clues.stem: Oligopoly theory split: when two rival gas stations compete strictly by undercutting each other’s posted PUMP PRICE rather than output volume, which model applies?
clues.ahaFactoid: Joseph Bertrand’s 1883 critique showed price competition between just two identical rivals can slash profits right down to marginal cost!

clues.stem: Behavioral pricing showdown: why do shoppers treat $2.99 coffee as meaningfully cheaper than $3.00 coffee even though the difference is a single penny?
clues.ahaFactoid: Because brains scan prices left to right and stop decoding early, "2.99" registers mentally in the two-dollar bucket rather than three!

clues.stem: Global price paradox: why does an identical haircut cost $45 in Zurich vs. $5 in Hanoi even though shampoo and scissors trade at similar world prices?
clues.ahaFactoid: Because high-productivity export factories in rich countries bid up local wages, non-traded local services like haircuts and dining cost far more there!
